questions.question: An integer linear program has an objective, linear constraints and integrality requirements on its variables. How is its LP relaxation formed?
options: Remove the integrality requirements and the hardest constraints; keep the objective
Remove the integrality requirements; keep the objective and all other constraints
Keep all constraints, but replace the objective by a simpler linear function
Keep everything, but round each variable to the nearest integer after solving

questions.question: An integer model contains a binary variable $x_j\in\{0,1\}$. Which restriction on $x_j$ does the LP relaxation use?
options: $x_j\ge0$, with $x_j$ continuous
$x_j\in\{0,1\}$, as binary choices stay
$0\le x_j\le1$, with $x_j$ continuous
No restriction at all, $x_j$ free

questions.question: For an integer linear program, let $F_I$ be its set of integer-feasible decisions and $F_R$ the feasible set of its LP relaxation. How are $F_I$ and $F_R$ related?
options: $F_R$ is contained in $F_I$
$F_I$ and $F_R$ have no point in common
$F_I$ is contained in $F_R$
$F_I$ and $F_R$ are always equal

questions.question: An integer minimization model has optimal value $z_{IP}$, and its LP relaxation has optimal value $z_{LP}$. How do they compare?
options: $z_{LP}\le z_{IP}$: the relaxed value is a lower bound
$z_{LP}\ge z_{IP}$: the relaxed value is an upper bound
$z_{LP}=z_{IP}$: both models share their constraints
No relation: the two models have different variables

questions.question: The LP relaxation of an integer model is solved, and the relaxed optimal solution happens to satisfy every integrality restriction of the original model. What follows?
options: It is feasible for the integer model, but not necessarily optimal
It only gives a bound; the integer model must still be solved
It is optimal only if it is also a corner of the integer region
It is optimal for the integer model, since it attains the bound

questions.question: For the integer model $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, which point is feasible for the LP relaxation but not for the integer model?
A mixed model requires $x_1$ to be integer, while $x_2$ is continuous, with constraints $x_1+x_2\le5$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. What does its LP relaxation change?
options: It drops the integrality of $x_1$; nothing else changes
It drops $x_1+x_2\le5$; the variables stay as they were
It makes $x_2$ integer as well, to treat both alike
It drops $x_1,x_2\ge0$ and the integrality of $x_1$

questions.question: For an integer maximization model with optimal value $z_{IP}$ and LP relaxation value $z_{LP}$, why does $z_{IP}\le z_{LP}$ hold?
options: $z_{LP}$ is a maximum over a set containing all integer decisions
The relaxation is easier to solve, so its value is higher
LP optima lie at corners, and corners have higher values
Integer points are rare in the region, so their values tend to be low

questions.question: The LP relaxation of an integer production model has optimal solution $(3.5,1.25)$. What role can this solution play for the integer model?
options: It can be implemented, as it satisfies every linear constraint
Its value bounds the integer optimum; it is not a valid plan
It has no use, as fractional solutions are meaningless
It shows that the integer model is infeasible

questions.question: For the binary model $\max 5x_1+4x_2+3x_3$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2+x_3\le4$, $x_1,x_2,x_3\in\{0,1\}$, the LP relaxation has optimal solution $(1,\tfrac{1}{3},1)$. What is its value, and what does it bound?
options: $\tfrac{28}{3}$, a lower bound on the optimal binary value
8, an upper bound on the binary optimum
12, an upper bound on the binary optimum
$\tfrac{28}{3}$, an upper bound on the binary optimum

questions.question: For the binary model $\max 5x_1+4x_2+3x_3$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2+x_3\le4$, $x_1,x_2,x_3\in\{0,1\}$, a student relaxes each $x_j\in\{0,1\}$ to $x_j\ge0$ only. The resulting LP has optimum $(0,0,4)$ with value 12. What does this show?
options: The bound 12 is invalid, as $(0,0,4)$ is not binary
Dropping $x_j\le1$ weakens the bound from $\tfrac{28}{3}$ to 12
The bound is unchanged, as 12 equals $\tfrac{28}{3}$ rounded up
$(0,0,4)$ is optimal for the binary model with value 12

questions.question: For the integer model $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the LP relaxation has value 13, and the integer point $(3,1)$ is feasible with value 11. What can be concluded about the integer optimal value $z_{IP}$?

For $\max x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le4$, $x_1\le2.5$, $x_2\le2.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, an LP solver returns the relaxed optimum $(2.5,1.5)$ with value 4. Does this fractional result mean $z_{IP}<4$?
options: Yes: a fractional relaxed optimum forces a strict gap
Yes: integer optima are always below relaxed values
No: the integer point $(2,2)$ is feasible with value 4
No: but only because the model is a minimization

questions.question: A modeller builds a bound for an integer maximization model in two ways: (a) remove integrality and also drop one constraint; (b) remove integrality and replace the objective by a simpler one. Which gives a valid upper bound on $z_{IP}$?
options: Only (a): its larger set still contains every integer decision
Only (b): a simpler objective still bounds the original
Both, since each removes integrality before solving
Neither, since the LP relaxation drops nothing but integrality

questions.question: For $\min 4x_1+3x_2$ subject to $4x_1+x_2\ge9$, $2x_1+2x_2\ge10$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the LP relaxation has value $\tfrac{49}{3}\approx16.33$. The point $(2,3)$ is feasible with cost 17. Is it optimal?
options: No: its cost 17 is strictly above the bound $\tfrac{49}{3}$
Yes: integer points have integer costs of at least 17
No: $(1,4)$, near the relaxed optimum, costs only 16
Yes, but only because $(2,3)$ is the relaxed optimum
